idiom_name: struct Orders: RandomAccessCollection over a private [Order] (value semantics)
implementation_notes: Swift's value semantics do the work other languages buy with unmodifiable wrappers: an Orders struct with a private storage array is copied on assignment, so a caller can never mutate the owner's collection, and mutating operations are `mutating func`s applied to the caller's own copy. Conforming to RandomAccessCollection (startIndex, endIndex, subscript, Index = Int) yields the entire sequence/collection surface - for-in, contains, map, filter, sorted, first - for free, which replaces the classic 'class that forwards every container method'. Invariants live in the initialiser and in the mutating methods, which throw when a rule is violated; a private stored property suppresses the synthesised memberwise initialiser, so provide an explicit validating init.
pitfalls: Copy-on-write means the first mutation after a value has been shared copies the whole buffer: mutating a long-lived collection element by element in a hot loop is O(n) per write until the buffer is uniquely referenced.
A private stored property suppresses the memberwise initialiser, so the validating init must be written explicitly - otherwise callers cannot construct the type at all.
startIndex/endIndex/subscript must agree for every state; non-contiguous or offset storage silently breaks every inherited algorithm.
Because the type is a value, a `let` binding cannot be mutated: model change as returning a new value rather than adding a class wrapper that reintroduces shared mutable state.
